newsitem.title: CHINA: China stock markets recover from crackdown shock.
newsitem.headline: China stock markets recover from crackdown shock.

text.p: China's stock markets have begun their recovery from the shock of an official crackdown, rising steadily since late last week on strong market fundamentals, analysts said on Wednesday.

With official Chinese statistics indicating healthy economic growth this year, further gains are expected despite the air of caution overhanging the market, which has pushed daily turnover down, they said.

By Wednesday's close, Shanghai's domestic A share index had risen 7.84 percent to 1,422.074 points against last Thursday's close, and the foreign currency B share index gained 4.33 percent 90.076 points.
In Shenzhen, the A share index added 9.42 percent to 474.17 points and the B index was up 5.07 percent to 158.81 points.
But the B share indices fell slightly on Wednesday on concerns over possible fresh crackdown measures, traders said.

Combined daily turnover on the two exchanges has fallen by about a third on average in the past few weeks compared with the volume in late April and early May when the markets were in a strong bull run, they said.
"Investors have recovered from the shock of an official crackdown last month with no new measures to cool down trading having been announced since early last week," one A share trader said.
"Market fundamentals are strong and the indices have the potential to go up further in the short term," he said.

"Recent official statistics have indicated the economy is growing in a healthy way," said a B share trader. "But investors have been cautious in building new positions, resulting in a fall in daily turnover."

In mid-May, Beijing took a series of measures to cool down trading on the overheating stock markets amid fears of a possible market collapse after prices on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges had risen more than 50 percent since the start of 1997.

The authorities banned state enterprises and listed firms from trading on the stock markets, set a huge quota for new A share issues and ordered the exchanges to halt trading in shares that had fluctuated sharply on alleged irregularities.

Before the crackdown, both Shanghai's A share index, at 1,578.611 points, and B index, at 99.312 points, were at three year highs. The Shenzhen A index was at a record high of 548.54 points, the B index, while not a record, was still considered high at 186.69 points.
Analysts said the rise in the past week was also due to a technical rebound after the crackdown measures saw share indices lose around 20 percent in three weeks.
"The loss during the crackdown has reduced speculative activities on the stock markets, paving the way for a technical rebound," said a broker with a major Chinese securities house.
"The rise in the past week has partly been led by shares which lost the most during the crackdown," he said.
"Looking at the strong economic data issued so far this year, I'd expect the stock markets to continue to rise in the short term," said a second broker.

"But both institutions and retail investors will be cautious not to allow the indices to surge in the short term, because they'd be afraid sharp gains could trigger fresh crackdown measures," he said.
Official statistics show China's gross domestic product (GDP) rose by a year-on-year 9.4 percent in the first three months of this year.
Retail price inflation rose a year-on-year 1.1 percent in April against 2.6 percent in the first three months and a year-on-year 6.1 percent for the whole of 1996.
Stock analysts said they believed that before July 1, when Hong Kong becomes part of China, share prices would at least regain the bulk of the ground lost during to the crackdown.
